title: Why Durga has many arms
hook: the second story begins: every god gives the goddess something of his own, and the mountain gives her a lion
carry: every god's power, held by one goddess
tomorrow: The demon who keeps changing shape

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vishnu slept on the waters until Brahma praised the goddess who was his sleep: the goddess's power moves even the gods.

A trident. A discus. A conch. A spear. A bow and two quivers of arrows. A thunderbolt, and a bell from an elephant's neck. A staff. A noose. Prayer beads and a water pot. A sword and a shield. An axe. Jewels, and a garland that never fades. A drinking cup. A snake to wear around the neck. And a lion. That's the inventory of the Devi Mahatmya's second story. It begins with the gods beaten by the buffalo demon Mahisha, their anger pouring out as light, and the light becoming a goddess. So what does everyone give her?
screen: `A TRIDENT, A DISCUS, A CONCH.` → `A CUP, A SNAKE, A LION.` → `WHAT DOES EVERYONE GIVE HER?`

segments.voice: In the second chapter the gods line up to give, and each gift comes out of the giver's own thing. Shiva draws a trident from his trident. Vishnu brings a discus out of his discus. Varuna gives a conch and a noose. Agni, fire, gives a spear. Indra gives a thunderbolt from his own, and a bell from his elephant. Brahma gives prayer beads and a water pot. The sun fills the pores of her skin with his rays. Kubera, lord of wealth, gives a full drinking cup. And Himavat, the Himalaya itself, gives her a lion to ride. Notice the first gifts. Shiva, Vishnu and Indra don't hand over a spare; each draws a copy from his own power. She carries all of it at once. That's why the goddess Hindus know as Durga is shown with many arms, each hand holding a god's gift, riding a lion: for devotees she is the gods' combined power in one form. Then she laughs, long and loud, and the sky fills with the sound. The earth shakes, and the demons rush toward the noise and see her, filling the three worlds with light. Mahisha's generals come at her with armies. As she fights, the breaths she lets out become troops, beating drums and blowing conches. She breathes, and allies appear. Her lion stalks through the enemy, and the chapter ends with the armies in ruins, and Mahisha still to come.
screen: `EACH GIFT FROM THE GIVER'S OWN.` · `THE MOUNTAIN GIVES A LION.` · `MANY ARMS, EVERY GOD'S GIFT.` · `HER BREATHS BECOME ARMIES.` · then, large: `SHE CARRIES ALL OF IT AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Find an image of Durga, in a home shrine, on your phone, or in your mind. Look at it slowly, hand by hand: the trident, Shiva's; the discus, Vishnu's; the conch, Varuna's; and under her, the mountain's lion. Then take her in whole, all of it at once. Hindus call this darshan: seeing the deity, and, many say, being seen. If you pray, greet her in your own words; if you don't, simply look.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its second story: a goddess armed with each god's own gift, riding the mountain's lion, whose breaths become armies.
Your line: every god's power, held by one goddess. Each gave from his own. That's today, done.

notes: Day 1054 (year three, 'the ranges ahead') already told the gods' light becoming the goddess and the trident and discus; this day acknowledges that and takes a new angle: the full inventory of gifts, her laugh, and her breaths becoming troops.

Gift list paraphrased from chapter 2: Shiva trident; Vishnu discus; Varuna conch and noose; Agni spear (śakti); Maruts (wind) bow and quivers (in the hook, not attributed in the teach); Indra thunderbolt and bell from Airavata; Yama staff; Brahma rosary and water pot; Surya rays in her pores; Kala sword and shield; the milk ocean jewels and unfading garments; Vishvakarma axe; Kubera a cup (of wine/drink) ever full; Himavat the lion; Shesha a serpent necklace. Some versions differ in small details; confirm the list.
Hook mentions 'a cup of wine' (Kubera's pānapātra). Confirm whether to say 'a drinking cup' instead.
'Her breaths become troops': the sighs (niśvāsa) she breathes out in battle become hundreds of thousands of gaṇas; the number is not spoken. Confirm.
Practice is an invitation to gratitude; it borrows the text's image of carrying every gift at once.
